title: The Village With No Name: Bruegel, the Alps, and the House of the Four Winds
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Breda, the birthplace van Mander names
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no baptismal record survives and the year is worked backward from the 1551 guild entry, with estimates running c. 1525-1530
stops.campa: Karel van Mander, writing thirty-five years after the painter is dead, says he was born in a village called Brueghel near Breda, and gives no year at all. No baptismal register survives. No village of that name has been found on any map of Brabant. The date of about 1525 is arithmetic run backward from the guild register that admits him a master in 1551. Breda in these years is a Nassau town in the Duchy of Brabant, sold to the dukes two centuries before, its market square the largest for miles around.
stops.quote: Bruegel was born in a village (dorp) near Breda called 'Brueghel'
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), as rendered in the Wikipedia article 'Pieter Bruegel the Elder'
sources: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), Life of Pieter Bruegel
suggested_refs: Van Mander's 1604 life of Bruegel, the sole source for the Breda tradition

stops.name: Bree, the rival birthplace in Limburg
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the same undocumented window as the Breda claim, which it contradicts
stops.campa: Flemish scholars have long put the birth somewhere else: at Grote-Brogel, a hamlet beside the small Limburg town of Bree, whose older name could as easily have given the painter his. The two traditions cannot both be true and neither carries a document. Van Mander wrote first and is followed by most of the literature; the Limburg claim rests on the place name and on local memory. Where the child actually opened his eyes, no document says. Bree keeps its claim in signage; Breda keeps its own.
sources: Manfred Sellink, Bruegel: The Complete Paintings (2007)
Local Limburg tradition as summarized in modern Bruegel scholarship
suggested_refs: Grote-Brogel and Kleine-Brogel, the Limburg hamlets advanced against Breda

stops.name: Antwerp, the workshop of Pieter Coecke van Aelst
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; van Mander's account only, with no contract and no dated year
stops.campa: Van Mander places the apprenticeship with Pieter Coecke van Aelst: painter, architect, translator of Serlio into Dutch, designer of tapestry cartoons for the emperor's court. No contract survives, and the guild registers do not enter the boy as anyone's pupil. The support for it is circumstantial. He will marry Coecke's daughter thirteen years later; he handles a print design like a man taught young to do it; and Coecke's shop published as readily as it painted, which is the trade Bruegel goes into. Coecke dies in Brussels on 6 December 1550.
suggested_refs: Coecke's Dutch edition of Serlio, the channel by which Italian architectural forms reached Antwerp workshops

stops.name: Mechelen, the glovemakers' altarpiece
stops.date_confidence: attested; guild and city records date the commission 1550-1551
stops.campa: The first hard trace of him at work is not a painting but a subcontract. Records at Mechelen have him assisting the painter Peeter Baltens on a large altarpiece for the glovemakers' guild, Bruegel taking the wings while Baltens takes the central panel. At about twenty-five he is a hired hand on another man's commission, in a town that specialized in cheap water-based painting on linen. He will come back to that technique in his last four years, for the pictures painted on cloth. The altarpiece is lost.
sources: Mechelen guild and city archives, cited in Sellink, Bruegel: The Complete Paintings (2007)
suggested_refs: The Mechelen trade in Tuchlein painting, distemper on linen, and its survival rate

stops.name: Antwerp, entered in the Liggeren as a free master
stops.date_confidence: attested; the guild year 1551, exact month not given by the register
stops.campa: The Liggeren, the register of the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke, enters Peeter Brueghels as a free master in the guild year 1551. It is the first date in this life that rests on a document rather than on a biographer's memory. A free master may take commissions, sign in his own name, keep apprentices, and sell without another man's stamp on the work. Antwerp in 1551 is the richest port in northern Europe and the largest market for pictures anywhere in it. Within a year of gaining the right to sell there, he leaves and walks south.
sources: Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke, Liggeren, 1551 entry
suggested_refs: The Liggeren of the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke, published by Rombouts and Van Lerius

stops.name: Lyon, the money road south
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no document places him in Lyon and the year is inferred from the journey's brackets
stops.campa: The road south that Netherlandish painters and merchants take runs through Champagne to Lyon, where the banking houses sit and where a traveler changes his money for Italy. No document names Bruegel here. He is placed on this road by its shape and by the company such a man would have kept. Clovio's inventory in Rome will later list a view of Lyon among the works by him. Whether he made it going south, coming back, or from another man's drawing without ever standing in the city, nobody can now say.
suggested_refs: The Antwerp-Lyon-Italy commercial route used by northern artists in the 1550s

stops.name: The Alps, the crossing that becomes the education
stops.date_confidence: attested for the crossing, reconstruction for the pass and the month; the Great Saint Bernard is a plausible route laid over a journey that certainly happened
stops.campa: He draws as he climbs: pen and ink sheets of rock walls, valleys dropping away below the path, weather coming across a ridge, all of it taken from the thing itself and not from another man's drawing. What survives of them is in the British Museum and the Louvre. Which pass he used is nowhere recorded. The sheets carry dates; the route is not on them. Fifteen years later the same rock forms will stand behind three hunters coming home over a ridge in Brabant, in a country that has no mountains in it.
stops.quote: swallowed all the mountains and rocks and spat them out again as panels on which to paint
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), Life of Pieter Bruegel
sources: Alpine landscape drawings, British Museum and Louvre
Nadine Orenstein, ed., Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints (Metropolitan Museum, 2001)
suggested_refs: The dated Alpine pen drawings of 1552-1554, the only physical record of the southward journey

stops.name: Waltensburg, the one Alpine sheet with a place name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; neither the month nor the identification of the site is secure
stops.campa: One Alpine sheet has been tied to an identifiable spot, a view in the Grisons associated with Waltensburg in the Surselva. The identification is not secure and the literature contradicts itself over it. The name points to the Surselva; the topography others read in the drawing points to the Domleschg, some thirty kilometres southeast near Thusis. The two valleys are not the same valley and the sheet cannot show both. It is one page of a mountain notebook whose other pages carry no place names at all. The drawing itself is not in doubt.
sources: Orenstein, ed., Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints (2001)
suggested_refs: The contested Grisons sheet and the Surselva versus Domleschg identification

stops.name: Reggio Calabria, the town burning across the strait
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the visit is inferred from a drawing and the traditional 1552 dating conflicts with the Ottoman raid chronology
stops.campa: He reaches the toe of Italy and looks across the narrows at Sicily. A drawing survives, known through copies, of Reggio burning and ships engaged in the strait, and it is the whole basis for putting him here at all. The older accounts have him witnessing an Ottoman bombardment in 1552. The chronicles of the Turkish raids on Calabria record Barbarossa firing the town in 1534 and Turgut Reis sacking it in June 1558, and nothing in the year the drawing is assigned to. Either he saw a fire no chronicler kept, or the sheet remembers a story rather than a day.
suggested_refs: Copies after the lost Bruegel drawing of Reggio in flames

stops.name: Messina, the crossing nobody can prove
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Sicilian leg rests on inference from later works and is disputed
stops.campa: Whether he crosses the water is unresolved. A lost drawing of a naval battle in the Strait of Messina, surviving in engraved and painted copies, shows ships and coastline with a precision that argues for a man who stood on a quay and counted them. No inventory, letter, or payment places him in Sicily, and Palermo rests on tradition alone. It could as easily have been drawn from the Calabrian shore, which on a clear day is near enough to read the harbour.
sources: Orenstein, ed., Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints (2001)
suggested_refs: The engraved copies after Bruegel's lost Strait of Messina drawing

stops.name: Naples, the bay and the panel that came later
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the visit is inferred from a painting now dated 1558-1562, well after the journey
stops.campa: He sees the bay, the fortress standing in the water, the half circle of the city under its mountain. What he makes of it comes much later. The panel of a naval battle in the Gulf of Naples in the Doria Pamphilj was painted in Antwerp between about 1558 and 1562, years after the journey, out of sketches and memory, and not every scholar grants it to him. The attribution is the argument for his having been here, and the argument goes in a circle: Naples is on the itinerary because of a picture, and the picture is his because of the itinerary.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Naval Battle in the Gulf of Naples'
suggested_refs: Naval Battle in the Gulf of Naples, Galleria Doria Pamphilj, Rome

stops.name: Rome, working beside Giulio Clovio
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Rome stay is documented, the inventory recording it is normally cited as 1577
stops.campa: In Rome he works beside Giulio Clovio, the Croatian miniaturist who illuminates for cardinals, and this is the one leg of the Italian journey a document supports. Clovio dies in January 1578. The inventory drawn up with his will lists works by Pietro Brugole in his rooms, among them a picture the two of them made together, a Tower of Babel painted on ivory, and a view of Lyon. That list is what survives of the friendship. Every one of the six works named on it has since disappeared.
suggested_refs: Clovio's will and inventory, the documentary anchor of Bruegel's Italian years

stops.name: The Brenner, going home with the drawings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the return route and its month are inferred from dated works bracketing the journey
stops.campa: Going north he crosses the mountains a second time. The route is reconstructed and not recorded, and the Brenner is the pass a man walking from Rome to the Netherlands would most likely take. The drawings from the southward crossing come home with him and are worked up in Antwerp into engraved sheets that a clerk can afford, so that the Alps enter the northern imagination as printed paper. He is about thirty years old, has been away perhaps two years, and has painted, so far as anybody can now demonstrate, nothing whatever.
sources: Orenstein, ed., Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints (2001)
suggested_refs: The Large Landscapes series, engraved from the Alpine sheets after the return

segments.name: The House of the Four Winds

stops.name: Antwerp, the press of Hieronymus Cock
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Large Landscapes are published this year
stops.campa: Back in Antwerp he goes to work for Hieronymus Cock, engraver and publisher, whose shop stands near the cathedral. Cock does not deal in panels. He sells prints by the hundred across Europe, and he commissions more than forty designs from Bruegel over the next decade, beginning with the Large Landscapes cut from the Alpine sheets. Most of the continent will know this work as ink on paper, at a price a merchant's clerk can pay, long before anyone abroad sees a painting. The shop is called In de Vier Winden, the House of the Four Winds.
sources: Hieronymus Cock's publication records and print inscriptions
Orenstein, ed., Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints (2001)
suggested_refs: In de Vier Winden / Aux Quatre Vents, Cock's shop, the largest print house in the Netherlands

stops.name: Antwerp, Big Fish Eat Little Fish issued under another man's name
stops.date_confidence: attested; drawn 1556, engraved and published 1557
stops.campa: Bruegel draws a beached fish split open, smaller fish spilling out of its belly, each of those with a smaller fish in its jaws, and a man in a boat pointing the lesson out to a boy. Cock has the design engraved and issues it inscribed Hieronymus Bos inventor. Hieronymus Bosch has been dead forty-one years. His name still sells prints and the living designer's does not yet, so the plate carries the dead man's. Cock paid for the design and Cock chose the name to put on it.
sources: Surviving 1557 engraving with the inscription 'Hieronymus Bos inventor'
Van Bastelaer and the New Hollstein Dutch and Flemish prints catalogues
suggested_refs: The 1557 engraving Big Fish Eat Little Fish and its false attribution line

stops.name: Antwerp, the first panel he signs
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the first securely dated painting; the month is arbitrary
stops.campa: He signs and dates a painting for the first time. Six years have passed since the guild admitted him and two since he began drawing for the press, and he has about twelve years left. The pictures are made for a narrow circle of Antwerp collectors rather than for a market: merchants, humanists, a few men with money and Latin. Van Mander says the painter himself had none of the last. From here on he paints for people who can come to the house and look at the thing on the easel. There are no altarpieces and no court commissions.
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), on Bruegel's education despite his humanist friendships
suggested_refs: The collectors' circle around Abraham Ortelius and Niclaes Jonghelinck in Antwerp

stops.name: Antwerp, the hells drawn for Cock
stops.date_confidence: attested for the series, which run c. 1556-1562; the year given is the middle of that run
stops.campa: Across these years he supplies the press with hells: the Seven Deadly Sins, the Last Judgement, temptations, plates crawling with fish-legged demons, walking eggs, houses that have mouths. The vocabulary is Hieronymus Bosch's, invented forty years earlier at 's-Hertogenbosch and by now common property in the Antwerp trade. Bruegel does not copy the older painter. He takes the grammar and says other things with it, and the sins he draws are ordinary ones committed by people in Flemish clothes. Van Mander in 1604 still calls him a second Bosch and means it as praise.
sources: Orenstein, ed., Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints (2001)
suggested_refs: The Seven Deadly Sins series, 1556-1558, published by Cock

stops.name: Antwerp, Netherlandish Proverbs painted
stops.date_confidence: attested; signed and dated on the panel
stops.campa: A village square holds more than a hundred sayings, performed literally by the people standing in it. A man bangs his head against a brick wall. Another casts roses before swine. A woman hangs a blue cloak over her husband, which is to say she deceives him, and a print of that subject the year before had already carried the line about the world's follies. Nothing in the panel is labelled and nothing is explained. The viewer is expected to know every proverb before he arrives, and to find his own among them without any help.
stops.quote: Die blau huicke is dit meest ghenaemt / Maer des weerelts abuisen het beter betaempt
stops.quote_source: Inscription on Frans Hogenberg's 1558 engraving of the Blue Cloak composition; glossed as 'Often called The Blue Cloak, this could better be called The World's Follies'
sources: Signed and dated panel, Gemaeldegalerie Berlin
suggested_refs: Frans Hogenberg's 1558 Blue Cloak engraving, the composition's immediate predecessor

stops.name: Antwerp, The Battle Between Carnival and Lent painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; signed and dated, month arbitrary
stops.campa: The square is split down the middle. On one side a fat man rides a beer barrel with a pie for a helmet and a spit for a lance. On the other a gaunt woman on a chair drawn by a monk and a nun levels a baker's peel with two herrings on it. Behind them stand the tavern and the church, and between the two runs the ordinary business of a town that has to live with both of them. Feast and fast joust in front of a crowd that is largely not watching, and the panel takes no side between them. It is painted the same year as the Proverbs and at nearly the same size.
sources: Signed and dated panel, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna
suggested_refs: The Vienna panel of Carnival and Lent, companion in scale to the Berlin Proverbs

stops.name: Antwerp, Children's Games painted
stops.date_confidence: attested; signed and dated on the panel
stops.campa: Around eighty games have been catalogued in the panel, and some accounts run past ninety: hoops, stilts, knucklebones, leapfrog, blind man's buff, a girl walking on her hands against a wall, boys riding a fence rail. The children fill the street to the horizon and there is no adult anywhere in the picture. The faces are not childish. They work at their games with the concentration of men at a trade. How many children are in the crowd altogether has never been settled, and the figures quoted do not agree with one another.
sources: Signed and dated panel, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna
suggested_refs: The catalogue of eighty identified games in the Vienna panel

stops.name: Antwerp, The Triumph of Death painted
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the panel is undated and c. 1562 is a stylistic estimate
stops.campa: An army of skeletons comes over a burnt landscape driving the living toward a trap lined with coffin lids. A king dies with his barrels of gold still in reach. A cardinal is helped along by a skeleton wearing a cardinal's hat. Two lovers at the lower right go on playing the lute, not having noticed anything. Ships burn in the bay, a wheel turns on its pole, a bell rings on a bare hill. The panel carries no date and the year assigned to it is an estimate made from how it is painted.
suggested_refs: The medieval Dance of Death tradition behind the Prado panel

stops.name: Antwerp, The Fall of the Rebel Angels painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; signed and dated, month arbitrary
stops.campa: Michael in gold armour drives the rebel host out of heaven, and the falling angels turn into other things as they drop: a butterfly's wing, a fish with legs, a fruit that splits open into a face. It is the most nearly Boschian panel he ever paints and the closest he comes to a doctrinal subject. For a long stretch of its history the picture was catalogued as a work of Hieronymus Bosch outright, and it hangs today in Brussels, a city he had not yet moved to when he painted it. The signature along the lower edge settled the question.
sources: Signed and dated panel, Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels
Wikipedia, 'The Fall of the Rebel Angels (Bruegel)'
suggested_refs: The Brussels panel's long misattribution to Bosch

stops.name: Antwerp, the servant girl and the tally stick
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; van Mander's anecdote carries no date and is placed loosely in the early 1560s
stops.campa: Van Mander tells a story with no document under it. In Antwerp the painter keeps house with a servant girl who lies habitually, and he cuts a notch in a tally stick for each lie, meaning to confront her with the whole stick when it fills. His prospective mother-in-law, the miniaturist Mayken Verhulst, will not have her daughter married into that household and makes the move to Brussels a condition of the match. One writer, thirty-five years after the fact, is the entire evidence, and he does not say whether the stick ever filled.
stops.quote: a very quiet and prudent man. He was a man of few words, but he was very droll in society, and he loved to make people jump with the unexpected jests and noises that he thought up.
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), Life of Pieter Bruegel
suggested_refs: Van Mander's anecdotes of Bruegel's Antwerp household, uncorroborated by any other source

segments.name: Brussels, the Marriage and the Tower

stops.name: Brussels, the deposition for marriage registered
stops.date_confidence: attested for the registration of the deposition; the wedding itself is dated only to 1563
stops.campa: On 25 July 1563 a deposition for marriage is registered in Brussels between Pieter Bruegel and Mayken Coecke, daughter of the master he is said to have trained under and of the miniaturist Mayken Verhulst. The church records the intention and not the day, which is why the marriage has no date and the paperwork does. He is somewhere near forty and she is a good deal younger. Thirteen years after Pieter Coecke van Aelst was buried, his workshop takes the pupil in as a son-in-law. The wedding follows sometime within the year.
sources: Brussels parish registration, cited in Wikipedia, 'Pieter Bruegel the Elder'
suggested_refs: The Kapellekerk marriage registers for 1563

stops.name: Brussels, the house on the Hoogstraat
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move in 1563; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: He leaves Antwerp for good and takes a house on the Hoogstraat in the Marolles, the low quarter beneath the Coudenberg where the government sits. Antwerp was the market. Brussels is the seat of Margaret of Parma's regency and of Cardinal Granvelle, who owns work of his. He will live here six years, paint nearly everything he is now known for, and be buried a few streets away. The house on the Hoogstraat is still standing and is shown to visitors as the Bruegelhuis, on evidence that is respectable rather than conclusive.
suggested_refs: The Bruegelhuis, Hoogstraat 132, Brussels

stops.name: Brussels, Dulle Griet painted
stops.date_confidence: attested since the 2018 restoration read the inscription as 1563; the panel was previously dated 1561
stops.campa: An armoured peasant woman with a sword and a bundle of plunder strides toward the mouth of hell, past a giant spooning coins out of his own backside, while behind her other women beat devils with kitchen implements. The picture was read for generations as the work of 1561, made in Antwerp. Restoration in 2018 recovered the inscription and found 1563, which moves it across the whole hinge of the life and into the first months in Brussels. It hangs today in a house museum in Antwerp, in the city he had just left.
sources: Museum Mayer van den Bergh, Antwerp
suggested_refs: The 2018 restoration report on Dulle Griet and its redating

stops.name: Brussels, The Tower of Babel painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; signed and dated, month arbitrary
stops.campa: The tower rises out of a Flemish harbour city in seven diminishing storeys, arcade on arcade, cranes still working the upper courses while the lower ones have already begun to lean. Its brickwork and its arches are Roman: he has stood inside the Colosseum. The building is a construction site and not a ruin, and what is wrong with it is structural rather than moral. At the lower left a king inspects the works, and the masons put down their tools and kneel to him in the dust.
stops.quote_source: Signature and date on The Tower of Babel, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna
sources: Signed and dated panel, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna
suggested_refs: Jan van Eyck's Saint Barbara of 1437, KMSKA Antwerp, seated before a tower still under construction, read as a pictorial ancestor of the motif

stops.name: Brussels, The Procession to Calvary painted
stops.date_confidence: attested; signed and dated on the panel
stops.campa: Some five hundred figures cross a Brabant landscape on what looks like a market day, and the man carrying the cross through the middle of them is nearly impossible to pick out. The crowd is walking out to watch an execution and most of it is talking about something else. In the foreground, painted larger and in an older manner, the mourning women grieve as though they were in a different picture, which in effect they are. The soldiers herding the rest wear the red tunics of the Habsburg mounted police.
stops.quote: [Bruegel] painted much that simply could not be painted. All of the works by our Bruegel always imply more than they depict.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Ortelius, on his friend, as quoted in the TheArtStory biography of Bruegel
sources: Signed and dated panel, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna
suggested_refs: The Vienna Procession to Calvary and its Habsburg red-coat cavalry

stops.name: Brussels, The Adoration of the Magi painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; signed and dated, month arbitrary
stops.campa: A tall narrow panel, and for once he comes close in. There is no landscape and no distant crowd, only the press of bodies around the manger. The kings are ugly, the soldiers behind them are uglier, and the gifts held out are elaborate goldsmith's work. A man at the Virgin's shoulder whispers into Joseph's ear and Joseph listens. Mary looks down at the child. This is the only picture in which Bruegel puts the viewer inside the group rather than on a hill above it.
sources: Signed and dated panel, National Gallery, London
suggested_refs: The London Adoration of the Magi, his only close-focus religious figure group

stops.name: Brussels, a first son born
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year from baptismal record; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A first son is born in the Brussels house and given his father's name. He will spend a working life of fifty years in Antwerp reproducing his father's compositions out of drawings and prints kept in the family: winter landscapes with bird traps, peasant weddings, proverbs, some fourteen hundred pictures with a plausible connection to his studio. One composition alone, the winter landscape with the bird trap, survives in at least sixty versions from that workshop. Almost everything the seventeenth century called Bruegel came through it. He is five years old when his father dies.
sources: Baptismal and parish records, standard Bruegel family record
suggested_refs: The output of Pieter Brueghel the Younger's Antwerp copying workshop, 1580s to 1638

segments.name: The Twelve Months of the Year

stops.name: Ter Beke, the cycle hung in Jonghelinck's villa
stops.date_confidence: attested through the 1566 pledge inventory, which fixes ownership and gives the terminus for the cycle's completion
stops.campa: Niclaes Jonghelinck, an Antwerp merchant with a country house called Ter Beke outside the walls, commissions a cycle of the year and hangs it in a room built for it. Ter Beke is gone, and the district of Antwerp that grew over the site kept the name. In 1566 he pledges his whole collection to the city as security for another man's tax debt, and the notary's list names sixteen Bruegels in the house, among them the twelve Months of the Year. That document, drawn up to secure a loan, is the reason the cycle can be dated at all.
sources: 1566 Antwerp inventory of Jonghelinck's collection pledged to the city
suggested_refs: The 1566 Jonghelinck pledge document naming sixteen paintings by Bruegel

stops.name: Brussels, The Hunters in the Snow painted
stops.date_confidence: attested; signed and dated on the panel
stops.campa: Three hunters come over a ridge into deep snow with one fox between them and a pack of thin dogs at their heels. Below, women burn straw at a fire outside an inn, skaters cut the frozen ponds, a bird trap is propped in a yard, and a bird crosses the valley toward mountains that do not exist anywhere in Brabant. He drew those mountains in the Alps thirteen years before, and they have been standing behind his weather ever since. Everything in the panel goes the same way, down and to the right, along the diagonal the hunters are already walking. The picture is one panel out of a set of six.
sources: Signed and dated panel, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna
suggested_refs: The Alpine drawings of 1552-1554 reused in the winter panel of the Months

stops.name: Brussels, the surviving panels of the Months
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the cycle; the individual panels are not separately dated
stops.campa: Four more survive. The hay harvest, with three women walking straight at the viewer carrying rakes. The grain harvest, with a reaper asleep on his back under a tree while the others eat bread and curds. The return of the herd, cattle driven down a hillside under a bruised sky. The gloomy day, all storm and pruned willows and a child wearing a paper crown. The 1566 document calls the set the twelve Months of the Year, and the reading now accepted is six panels of two months each, five of them still in existence, in Vienna, New York, and Prague.
sources: Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna; Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; Lobkowicz Collection, Prague
suggested_refs: The missing sixth panel of the Months, unlocated

stops.name: Brussels, The Massacre of the Innocents painted
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the panel is undated and assigned to c. 1565-1567
stops.campa: Soldiers in Habsburg armour, led by a black-clad commander with a long white beard, seal off a snowbound Flemish village and pull children out of the houses. It is a biblical subject, and nobody living in the Netherlands of the 1560s could have looked at it as only that. The emperor Rudolf II, who owned the panel, had the murdered children painted out and turned into bundles, food, and animals, so that the soldiers appear to be plundering rather than killing. Conservation confirmed the overpaint in 1998 and left it where it was.
suggested_refs: The 1998 conservation findings on Rudolf II's overpainting of the Royal Collection panel

stops.name: Brussels, The Wine of Saint Martin's Day painted
stops.date_confidence: inferred; dated on stylistic grounds to c. 1565-1568, with no signature legible until 2010
stops.campa: A crowd of more than a hundred swarms up an enormous vat of new wine, tipping it, drinking out of hats and jugs and cupped hands, hauling each other down by the legs, while at the right the saint on his white horse cuts his cloak in half for a beggar and not one of them turns to look. It is painted in glue tempera on linen, a cheap and fragile technique that almost never survives four centuries. The picture hung in Spain uncatalogued until X-rays in 2010 found fragments of a signature under the surface.
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Wine of Saint Martin's Day'
suggested_refs: The 2010 Prado technical examination that identified the Tuechlein as a Bruegel

stops.name: Brussels, The Land of Cockaigne painted
stops.date_confidence: attested; signed and dated on the panel
stops.campa: Three men lie flat on their backs around a tree with a table top fixed to it: a scholar with his books and his fur, a soldier with his lance dropped in the grass, a peasant with his flail. A pig runs past with the carving knife already stuck in its flank. A roof is tiled with pies. An egg walks by with a spoon in it. The paradise the folk story promises and the punishment for wanting it are the same picture. At the top left a fourth man eats his way in through a hill of porridge.
sources: Signed and dated panel, Alte Pinakothek, Munich
suggested_refs: The Cockaigne folk tradition in sixteenth-century Netherlandish literature

stops.name: Brussels, The Peasant Wedding and The Peasant Dance painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1567 on both panels; the Peasant Dance is normally given as c. 1567 and the two are often wrongly bracketed under 1568
stops.campa: A barn, a plank door carried in as a serving tray, bowls of custard passed down a table, a bagpiper watching the food go past him. The bride sits under a paper crown with her hands folded and her eyes shut, and the bridegroom cannot be identified in the picture with any certainty at all. He paints people he has watched closely and does not flatter them. In the dance panel the couples come at the viewer heavily, the bagpipe screaming, a church at the end of the street and a picture of the Virgin nailed to a tree that nobody is turning to look at.
stops.quote: In a wonderful manner Nature found and seized the man who in his turn was destined to seize her magnificently, when in an obscure village in Brabant she chose from among the peasants, as the delineator of peasants, the witty and gifted Pieter Bruegel and made him a painter to the lasting glory of our Netherlands.
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), opening of the Life of Pieter Bruegel
suggested_refs: The Vienna peasant panels and the debate over whether Bruegel mocked or recorded

stops.name: Brussels, The Blind Leading the Blind painted
stops.date_confidence: attested; signed and dated on the cloth
stops.campa: Six blind men cross a slope in a line, each with a hand on the shoulder or the staff of the man ahead of him, and the leader has already gone over into the water. The second is falling, his face turned up. The four behind have not yet felt it travel back down the line to them. Behind the whole row a church stands in a quiet village and the grass is in good order. The parable is one sentence long in Matthew and he has painted it as a sequence, six stages of one accident laid out left to right across a single cloth. It is distemper on linen, signed and dated 1568, and it is in Naples.
sources: Signed and dated work, Museo di Capodimonte, Naples
suggested_refs: Matthew 15:14 and the Netherlandish proverb tradition behind the Naples cloth

stops.name: Brussels, The Magpie on the Gallows painted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; signed and dated, month arbitrary
stops.campa: A small panel: a gallows standing on a knoll with a magpie perched on the crossbeam, peasants dancing underneath it, a wide sunlit river valley opening away behind, and at the bottom left a man squatting in the bushes. Van Mander says the painter left this picture to his wife by name, and gives his own reading of what the bird was doing up there. In the Netherlands of 1568 a gallows set in a landscape did not require a caption. The dancers have their backs to the thing they are dancing under, and behind them the valley is the best weather he ever painted.
stops.quote: he was referring by the magpie to the gossips, whom he would like to see hanged.
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), Life of Pieter Bruegel
suggested_refs: The Darmstadt panel, the only picture van Mander says Bruegel willed to a named person

stops.name: Brussels, a second son born
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year from baptismal record; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A second son is born in the Hoogstraat house a year before his father's death. He will have no memory of him whatever, and will become the most commercially successful painter the family produces: flowers, silk, small copper panels crowded with animals, handling so fine that Antwerp calls him Velvet Brueghel. He will paint landscape into Rubens's pictures and Rubens will paint figures into his. Their grandmother, Mayken Verhulst, teaches both boys watercolour and gouache before either of them is allowed near oil.
sources: Baptismal and parish records, standard Bruegel family record
suggested_refs: The Jan Brueghel and Rubens collaborations of the 1600s

stops.name: Brussels, the order to burn the drawings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; van Mander's account only, undated beyond the fact of the final illness
stops.campa: Dying, according to van Mander, he tells his wife to burn a number of drawings, ones whose inscriptions could be used against her once he was no longer there to answer for them. No list of those sheets exists. Nothing corroborates the story, which comes from a writer who never met him and set it down thirty-five years later. What was on those sheets, and whether a careful man in Brussels in 1569 had reason to fear them, is not a question the record can answer.
stops.quote: which were too sharp or sarcastic
stops.quote_source: Karel van Mander, Het Schilder-boeck (1604), on the drawings Bruegel had burned
suggested_refs: Van Mander's deathbed passage, the origin of the lost-drawings tradition

stops.name: Brussels, death in the Hoogstraat house
stops.date_confidence: attested; burial record and epitaph give 9 September 1569
stops.campa: He dies in Brussels on 9 September 1569, in the house on the Hoogstraat. Nobody knows his birth year within five, so nobody knows his age; the usual estimate puts him in his middle forties. Measured from the first signed panel, the painting career lasted twelve years. He leaves a widow he married six years before, a son of five and a son of one, some forty surviving paintings, and a body of print designs already circulating across Europe under another man's imprint.
sources: Burial record, Church of Notre-Dame de la Chapelle, Brussels
suggested_refs: The Brussels burial record of September 1569

stops.name: Brussels, buried in the Kapellekerk
stops.date_confidence: attested for burial in 1569 at this church; the exact day of interment is not recorded
stops.campa: He is buried in the Church of Our Lady of the Chapel at the foot of the Marolles, a few minutes' walk from his own door. A modest funerary monument commemorates him there and is still standing. Tradition credits his sons with commissioning it and links it to the copy of Rubens's Christ Handing the Keys to Saint Peter that hangs in the church, though the church's own account asserts neither of those things. Five years after the burial his friend Abraham Ortelius, the cartographer, wrote a line about him into his album of friends.
stops.quote: the most perfect painter of his century
sources: Wikipedia, 'Church of Our Lady of the Chapel'
suggested_refs: Ortelius's album amicorum, and his remark that Bruegel's works always imply more than they depict

stops.name: Brussels, the boys go to their grandmother
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; van Mander records the grandmother's teaching without dating the arrangement
stops.campa: The widow and the two boys go to Mayken Verhulst: miniaturist, widow of Pieter Coecke van Aelst, and by van Mander's account the first teacher of both grandsons. The father's drawings and the family's stock of prints stay in the house, and out of them the elder boy will build a copying workshop that keeps the compositions in production for half a century. She puts brushes in the hands of a five-year-old and an infant, and the trade passes to a third generation without a contract or an indenture anywhere in it. Van Mander is the only source for the arrangement, and he does not say when it was made.
suggested_refs: Mayken Verhulst's role in transmitting the Coecke and Bruegel workshops to a third generation
